### Problem: Make Sum Divisible by P {#sec-hash-p5-b}

::: {.p-statement}
Given $a$ ($1 \le n \le 10^5$, $1 \le a_i \le 10^9$) and $p$ ($1 \le p \le 10^9$), remove the **shortest non-empty contiguous subarray whose removal makes the rest divisible by $p$** — or return $-1$ if impossible. **You may not remove the whole array.** (Answer $0$ when the sum is already divisible.)

Source: [LC 1590 · Make Sum Divisible by P](https://leetcode.com/problems/make-sum-divisible-by-p/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Let $R = \bigl(\sum a\bigr) \bmod p$. Removing the middle piece $a[\ell..r]$ is divisible-by-$p$ exactly when $\text{pref}_r - \text{pref}_{\ell-1} \equiv R \pmod p$, where $\text{pref}$ is the prefix-sum remainder array of @sec-pref — rearranged: $\text{pref}_{\ell-1} \equiv \text{pref}_r - R$. So for each right end $r$, you need the **latest** earlier prefix with remainder $(\text{pref}_r - R) \bmod p$, because latest ⇒ shortest window. A map from remainder to latest index answers it in one pass — @sec-hash-complement's seen table wearing @sec-pref's clothes; the bookkeeping rule `last = {0: -1}` says "prefix of length zero, remainder $0$, sits at index $-1$".
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Every window, checked.** For each $(\ell, r)$ with $r - \ell + 1 < n$, test $(\text{pref}_r - \text{pref}_{\ell-1}) \bmod p = R$; $O(n^2)$ — the honesty baseline and the *rule-checker* for the whole-array ban.
2. **Remainder → latest index.** One pass: maintain `pref`, look up `(pref - R) % p` in `last`, shrink `best`, then `last[pref] = i`. $O(n)$ expected.

**Invariant.** Before index $i$, `last[r]` holds the greatest $j < i$ with prefix remainder $r$ (and $-1$ for $r = 0$, the empty prefix); therefore $i - \text{last}[(\text{pref}_i - R)]$ is the shortest window *ending at $i$* that removes the right remainder.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Try every proper window

::: {.form-next}
Direct reading of the statement, with the ban made explicit: skip $(\ell, r) = (0, n-1)$. Running prefix remainders keep each test $O(1)$, so this is $O(n^2)$ — hopeless at $n = 10^5$, but it is the version whose *rules* (non-empty, not-whole) the fast form must match.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def min_subarray_brute(a, p):
    n = len(a)
    total = sum(a) % p
    if total == 0:
        return 0
    best = n + 1
    for i in range(n):
        run = 0
        for j in range(i, n):
            run = (run + a[j]) % p
            if run == total and j - i + 1 < n:   # proper window only
                best = min(best, j - i + 1)
    return best if best <= n else -1
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
using namespace std;

int minSubarrayBrute(vector<int>& a, int p) {
    int n = (int)a.size();
    long long total = 0;
    for (int x : a) total = (total + x) % p;
    if (total == 0) return 0;
    int best = n + 1;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        long long run = 0;
        for (int j = i; j < n; ++j) {
            run = (run + a[j]) % p;
            if (run == total && j - i + 1 < n) best = min(best, j - i + 1);
        }
    }
    return best <= n ? best : -1;
}
```
:::

#### Latest index per remainder

::: {.form-next}
Replace "every earlier $\ell$" by "the best earlier $\ell$": keep `last` = remainder → greatest index, seed `last[0] = -1` for windows starting at $0$, and at each $i$ query the complement $(\text{pref} - R) \bmod p$ before storing $i$ as the new record for `pref`. The whole-array ban is enforced at the end: at $i = n - 1$ the prefix remainder equals $R$, so the wanted remainder is $0$, which the seed `last[0] = -1` supplies — the scan *does* record the full window, of length $n$. Returning `best` only when `best < n` rejects it.
:::


::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-make-sum-divisible
def min_subarray(a, p):
    rem = sum(a) % p
    if rem == 0:
        return 0                         # nothing to remove
    last = {0: -1}                       # empty prefix sits at index -1
    pref, best = 0, len(a)
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        pref = (pref + x) % p
        want = (pref - rem) % p          # Python's % never goes negative
        if want in last:
            best = min(best, i - last[want])
        last[pref] = i                   # query BEFORE store: latest per remainder
    return best if best < len(a) else -1 # -1 = impossible (or would remove all)


for _ in range(2000):
    a = [random.randint(1, 12) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 9))]
    p = random.randint(2, 9)
    assert min_subarray(a, p) == min_subarray_brute(a, p)

assert min_subarray([3, 1, 4, 2], 6) == 1        # the LC examples
assert min_subarray([6, 3, 5, 2], 9) == 2        # the board sample
assert min_subarray([1, 2, 3], 3) == 0           # already divisible
assert min_subarray([1, 2, 3], 7) == -1          # LC: only the whole array works - banned
assert min_subarray([1, 2], 4) == -1             # the same situation, smaller
print("min_subarray OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr);
    int n; cin >> n; int p;
    vector<long long> a(n);                // sums reach 1e14 - long long (@sec-arr-cost)
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) cin >> a[i];
    cin >> p;
    long long total = 0;
    for (long long x : a) total = (total + x) % p;
    if (total == 0) { cout << 0 << '\n'; return 0; }
    unordered_map<long long, int> last;
    last[0] = -1;
    long long pref = 0;
    int best = n;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
        pref = (pref + a[i]) % p;
        long long want = (pref - total % p + p) % p;   // C++ % can go NEGATIVE: +p
        if (last.count(want)) best = min(best, i - last[want]);
        last[pref] = i;
    }
    cout << (best < n ? best : -1) << '\n';            // whole-array ban
}
```
:::
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Try every proper window** is $O(n^2)$ time, $O(1)$ space — $10^{10}$ operations at the limits, out (@sec-cx-budget). **Latest index per remainder** is $O(n)$ expected time and $O(\min(n, p))$ space; the map stores at most one entry per distinct remainder. Note what did *not* change versus @sec-pref: the algebra is still prefix-difference, just taken modulo $p$ so the table keys on remainders instead of sums.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Sum already divisible: $0$, returned before the scan.
- Impossible: the only window with the right remainder is the whole array, so `best` stays $n$ and the answer is $-1$. LC's example $[1, 2, 3]$ with $p = 7$ is exactly this; so is $[1, 2]$ with $p = 4$ in the asserts.
- $p = 1$: everything is divisible; form 2 returns $0$ at the guard.
- Negative values are outside this statement's constraints, but the two languages' `%` disagree on them anyway — the `+p` normalisation is a standing habit (@sec-hash-keys), not a one-off.
:::

::: {.practice}
- [LC 525 · Contiguous Array](https://leetcode.com/problems/contiguous-array/){difficulty="Medium"} — the key is a running balance ($+1$ for a one, $-1$ for a zero), and the *earliest* index per key gives the longest window.
- [CF 1426D · Non-zero Segments](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1426/D){rating="1500"} — a set of prefix sums seen since the last cut; a repeated prefix sum means a zero-sum segment, so cut and clear the set.
:::
